```{r setup, include=FALSE}
root <- normalizePath(if (file.exists("STAT525_Project.Rproj")) "." else "..")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = root)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
```

```{r analysis, include=FALSE}
source("R/02_economic_factors.R", local = TRUE)

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
}
change <- function(b) {
  paste(fmt(abs(b), 3), "MWh/person", if (b < 0) "lower" else "higher")
}
r2 <- function(fit) 100 * summary(fit)$r.squared

y <- county[[yvar]]
qt_y <- quantile(y, c(.25, .5, .75))
max_y <- which.max(y)
rho <- correlations["hdd100", "cdd100"]
weather_test <- anova(econ, full)

income_x <- model.frame(simple$income10k)$income10k
income_res <- residuals(simple$income10k)
sd_low <- sd(income_res[income_x <= quantile(income_x, .25)])
sd_high <- sd(income_res[income_x >= quantile(income_x, .75)])
```

## Part A. Exploration and simple regressions

How does modeled residential electricity use per person vary across U.S.
counties with heating and cooling demand, median household income, and
unemployment? Each county receives equal weight. Among `r fmt(nrow(county), 0)`
counties, median electricity use was `r fmt(qt_y[2])` MWh/person, with the
middle half between `r fmt(qt_y[1])` and `r fmt(qt_y[3])`. Saad's energy
section shows the distribution of this shared response.

Heating degree days (HDD) and cooling degree days (CDD) sum daily temperature
departures below and above 65°F, respectively. We used a county's 2016 totals
only when all 366 daily temperatures were available. The FIPS join matched
`r fmt(sum(!is.na(weather_row)), 0)` energy counties to weather records, and
`r fmt(nobs(simple$hdd100), 0)` had usable annual totals. Income is the
2012–2016 ACS five-year estimate in 2016 dollars. Unemployment is the BLS
2016 annual-average rate.

```{r distributions, out.width="85%", fig.cap="Figure 1. County distributions of each predictor. Panel titles give the number of counties with observations."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(out, "hist.png")), rel_path = FALSE)
```

The income and unemployment distributions have long upper tails. For example,
`r county$county_state_name[which.max(county$unemployment)]` had
`r fmt(max(county$unemployment, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`% unemployment, compared
with a county median of `r fmt(median(county$unemployment, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`%.
Among counties with complete weather records, median HDD and CDD were
`r fmt(100 * median(county$hdd100, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` and
`r fmt(100 * median(county$cdd100, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` degree-days.
On the response side, `r county$county_state_name[max_y]` had the highest
electricity use at `r fmt(y[max_y])` MWh/person. We retained unusual
observations whenever the required predictors were available.

```{r scatter, out.width="85%", fig.cap="Figure 2. Residential electricity use against each predictor. Each dot is one county. The solid line is the simple linear fit and the dashed line is a locally smoothed trend."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(out, "scatter.png")), rel_path = FALSE)
```

```{r simple-results}
knitr::kable(
  simple_table, digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2),
  col.names = c("Predictor", "Counties", "Slope", "95% lower", "95% upper",
                "R² (%)", "Residual SE"),
  caption = "Table 1. Separate regressions. Slopes give MWh/person per predictor unit shown. Residual SE is in MWh/person. Intervals use ordinary least squares."
)
```

A $10,000 higher median household income was associated with fitted electricity
use that was `r change(coef(simple$income10k)[2])` in the income-only model.
Unemployment alone explained `r fmt(r2(simple$unemployment), 3)`% of the
variation. The HDD-only and CDD-only fits explained
`r fmt(r2(simple$hdd100), 1)`% and `r fmt(r2(simple$cdd100), 1)`%,
respectively, on the same weather-covered counties.

**Model checks.** A log-income fit explained `r fmt(r2(log_income), 1)`% of
the variation versus `r fmt(r2(simple$income10k), 1)`% on the dollar scale.
We retained income in $10,000 units for interpretation. Adding a squared CDD
term to the CDD-only model changed adjusted R² by
`r fmt(100 * (summary(cdd_curve)$adj.r.squared - summary(simple$cdd100)$adj.r.squared), 2)`
percentage points. Figure 2 shows where the smoothed trend departs from the
straight line and how many counties support the pattern.

Income-model residual SD was `r fmt(sd_low)` MWh/person in the lowest income
quartile and `r fmt(sd_high)` in the highest. The largest absolute standardized
residual in that fit was `r fmt(max(abs(rstandard(simple$income10k))), 1)`.
The wider spread at high incomes makes heteroskedasticity-robust intervals a
useful follow-up to the conventional intervals reported here. Neighboring
counties may also have correlated errors. The supporting plots below show the
residual and normal Q–Q checks for each fit.

```{r correlations}
short <- c("HDD", "CDD", "Income", "Unemployment")
dimnames(correlations) <- list(short, short)
knitr::kable(correlations, digits = 2,
             caption = "Table 2. Pearson correlations on the joint model sample.")
```

Among the `r fmt(nrow(joint), 0)` joint-model counties, HDD and CDD had
`r sprintf("r = %.2f", rho)`. A simple regression of one weather measure on
the other explains `r fmt(100 * rho^2, 1)`% of its variation. The variation
remaining after accounting for the other weather measure helps distinguish
the two slopes in the joint model.

## Part B. Do HDD and CDD add information beyond income and unemployment?

We fit an economic model with income and unemployment, then added HDD and CDD.
Both models used the same `r fmt(nrow(joint), 0)` counties. The economic model
explained `r fmt(r2(econ), 1)`% of the variation. Adding weather brought this
to **`r fmt(r2(full), 1)`%**, a gain of
**`r fmt(r2(full) - r2(econ), 1)` percentage points**. The joint model's
adjusted R² was `r fmt(summary(full)$adj.r.squared, 3)` and its residual
standard error was `r fmt(sigma(full))` MWh/person. The joint test for adding
HDD and CDD gave F(2, `r df.residual(full)`) = `r fmt(weather_test$F[2])`
with p-value `r format.pval(weather_test[["Pr(>F)"]][2], digits = 2, eps = .001)`.

```{r adjusted-results}
knitr::kable(
  adjusted_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Predictor", "Adjusted slope", "95% lower", "95% upper"),
  caption = "Table 3. Joint model slopes in MWh/person per unit shown, holding the other three predictors fixed. Intervals are model-based 95% confidence intervals."
)
```

At fixed HDD, income, and unemployment, an additional 100 CDD was associated
with fitted electricity use that was `r change(coef(full)["cdd100"])`.
At fixed weather and unemployment, a $10,000 higher median income was
associated with fitted electricity use that was `r change(coef(full)["income10k"])`.

`r joint$county_state_name[influential]` (FIPS `r joint$county_fips[influential]`)
had the largest Cook's distance in the joint fit. Omitting it in a sensitivity
check changed the CDD slope from `r fmt(coef(full)["cdd100"], 3)` to
`r fmt(coef(without_one)["cdd100"], 3)` MWh/person per 100 CDD.

These comparisons describe county averages. The climate findings apply to
counties with complete temperature records. Differences in housing and heating
fuel could also contribute to the associations. NREL used household income
categories in constructing its residential energy estimates, so part of the
income relationship may reflect how the response was modeled.
[NREL methodology](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy19osti/72748.pdf)
